entry.title: University of Utah Researchers Identify Mushroom Behind Lilliputian Hallucinations
entry.content:
ScienceDaily | sciencedaily.com | source

Researchers at the University of Utah used DNA sequencing to identify the mushroom Lanmaoa asiatica as the cause of Lilliputian hallucinations—vivid, detailed visions of miniature humans interacting with their surroundings—in Southwest China and the northern Philippines. Chemical and genetic testing revealed that the mushroom lacks known psychoactive compounds like psilocybin, pointing to an entirely unfamiliar hallucinogenic substance.

Genomic analysis of 53 specimens across the broader Lanmaoa genus also uncovered four previously unknown species, demonstrating how field research and museum collections can reveal new biological diversity. Isolating the mushroom's mysterious active compound could provide researchers with a novel tool to investigate the neurological mechanisms that generate complex visual hallucinations in humans.

entry.title: University of Warwick Researchers Challenge 40-Year Superconductor Assumption
entry.content:
ScienceDaily | sciencedaily.com | source

Researchers at the University of Warwick have discovered that copper-based cuprate superconductors, long assumed to possess a uniform crystal structure, actually contain a complex patchwork of different atomic arrangements. Using scanning three-dimensional X-ray diffraction at the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility, the team mapped interior structural variations and found boundary regions hundreds of times wider than previously expected.

Published in Physical Review Letters, the findings challenge four decades of scientific assumptions built on the premise of uniform interior structures. The unexpected internal complexity and unusually broad transition zones may actively interfere with electrical performance, indicating that prior bulk measurements and theoretical models will need to be reevaluated.

entry.title: ESO Astronomers Report Possible Detection of First Exosatellite in CD-35 2722 System
entry.content:
ScienceDaily | sciencedaily.com | source

Astronomers using the European Southern Observatory's Very Large Telescope have found evidence of a massive moon-like object in the CD-35 2722 star system. Rather than orbiting a planet, this Jupiter-mass object circles a brown dwarf, which in turn orbits a star about half the mass of the Sun.

Reported in Nature, the discovery complicates traditional astronomical classifications that sharply separate planets, stars, and natural satellites. Because no exomoon has yet been definitively confirmed, researchers hope upcoming facilities like the Extremely Large Telescope will help verify such unusual systems and clarify how they form.

entry.title: Yuezhuornis yangyuanensis Fossil Discovered in China Reveals Early Flightless Bird Lineage
entry.content:
ScienceDaily | sciencedaily.com | source

Researchers in China have discovered the fossil of a crow-sized bird named Yuezhuornis yangyuanensis that lived approximately 150 million years ago during the Late Jurassic period. Described in Nature, the specimen combines bird-like skeletal features with predatory dinosaur traits, including serrated teeth and sickle-shaped claws on its second toes.

Statistical comparisons of its limb proportions indicate that the species was ground-dwelling and likely incapable of flight, representing the earliest known example of a bird lineage losing its flying ability. The findings challenge the assumption that early avian evolution was strictly directed toward improved flight, demonstrating that prehistoric birds rapidly diversified into various ecological niches and terrestrial lifestyles.

entry.title: Dwarf Reedsnakes Use High-Speed Rolling to Escape Predators
entry.content:
ScienceDaily | sciencedaily.com | source

Dwarf reedsnakes native to Southeast Asia escape predators by rapidly rolling across the ground at speeds up to four times faster than their standard slithering movement. Researchers analyzing multi-angle video recordings found that these small reptiles reach peak forward velocities between 1.72 and 3.69 meters per second while executing the maneuver.

To achieve high-speed rolling without a mechanical wheel axle, the snakes coordinate complex body movements by alternating side-to-side strokes while keeping their heads remarkably stable and pointed forward. This specialized separation of function demonstrates how precise muscular control and behavioral innovation can enable forms of locomotion that seem physically improbable given an animal's anatomy.

entry.title: University of Strathclyde and Durham University Researchers Propose Mirror Life Detection Method
entry.content:
ScienceDaily | sciencedaily.com | source

Researchers from the University of Strathclyde and Durham University have proposed a detection method for "mirror life," a hypothetical form of life built from reversed molecular structures. The technique utilizes circularly polarized luminescence (CPL)—the same foundational concept used in 3D movie glasses—to analyze light emitted with specific left- and right-handed properties by specialized fluorescent probes attached inside cells.

Although mirror life does not currently exist, experts view its potential creation as a serious biosecurity concern because synthetic reversed organisms could interact unpredictably with Earth's ecosystems and evade natural defenses. The proposed CPL assay offers a contingency screening approach using ordinary biological samples, allowing scientists to develop detection capabilities and support potential future biosecurity regulations before any such organisms emerge.

entry.title: University of Chicago Researchers Develop Computational Framework for Spin Defect Internal Conversion
entry.content:
ScienceDaily | sciencedaily.com | source | hacker news

Researchers at the University of Chicago Pritzker School of Molecular Engineering have created a computational method to simulate the complete optical cycle and internal conversion processes of spin defects in materials like diamond and silicon carbide. By combining many-body wavefunctions with analytical non-adiabatic couplings, the framework maps how excited electronic states interact with atomic vibrations across hundreds of atoms.

Implemented within the open-source WEST simulation program, the approach resolved a long-standing discrepancy in silicon carbide by showing that internal conversion has a larger impact on excited triplet state lifetimes than previously estimated. This predictive capability could assist in designing better quantum qubits and materials for renewable energy storage, with ongoing efforts exploring machine learning to further enhance simulation efficiency.

An international research team led by the University of Queensland has compiled a unified dataset of 2,884 Type Ia supernovae, combining three decades of astronomical measurements into a single framework. The comprehensive catalog provides fresh evidence that dark energy may vary over time rather than remaining constant, challenging the central assumption of the standard cosmological model.

To ensure consistency across historical observations, the researchers applied updated analytical techniques and accounted for variables such as cosmic dust, galaxy masses, and gravitational lensing. These findings align with independent results from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument, offering additional impetus to investigate whether time-varying dark energy could eventually help reconcile general relativity with quantum physics.

Led by the National Astronomical Observatory of Japan, the international team captured detailed measurements showing that the Sun's magnetic canopy is far more complex and twisted than previously understood.

Operating from the stratosphere at an altitude of 35 kilometers during a 2024 mission, the observatory used its onboard SCIP near-infrared spectropolarimeter to measure magnetic fields across multiple layers of the solar atmosphere. These observations, supported by numerical simulations, offer new insight into how surface motions twist magnetic field lines and help heat the upper layers of the solar atmosphere.

entry.title: ETH Zurich Study on Asteroid Bennu Samples Reveals Early Solar System Formation History
entry.content:
ScienceDaily | sciencedaily.com | source

Researchers at ETH Zurich analyzing samples collected from asteroid Bennu by NASA's OSIRIS-REx mission have found that the asteroid formed near the water-ice line in the early Solar System about 4.5 billion years ago. Isotope analysis of iron, titanium, and chromium revealed that Bennu shares a close chemical relationship with asteroid Ryugu and rare CI meteorites, pointing to a hybrid origin from both inner and outer Solar System materials.

The findings challenge earlier assumptions that primitive asteroids originated exclusively in the outer Solar System. The researchers propose that Jupiter's rapid early growth acted as a structural barrier, limiting the movement of larger particles while allowing fine dust to mix near the water-ice boundary, preserving chemical signatures closely resembling the elemental composition of the Sun.

entry.title: Kadoa Report Finds Investor-Owned Utilities Charge 23% More For Electricity Than Public Providers
entry.content:
Hacker News Best | kadoa.com | hacker news

In 2025, residential electricity customers paid an average of 17.8 cents per kilowatt-hour at investor-owned utilities, compared to 14.5 cents at public utilities and 14.1 cents at co-ops. Since 2020, investor-owned utility prices increased by 34%, outpacing both public utility price growth of 19% and general inflation of 24%.

The widening price gap primarily developed between 2020 and 2023 during a broad energy price spike, with investor-owned rates rising 25% while nonprofit utility rates rose 11%. Investor-owned utilities build shareholder returns into their rate structures, whereas public utilities and co-ops operate without shareholders and often benefit from tax exemptions and tax-free borrowing.

entry.title: UNEP Releases Emissions Gap Report 2026 on 1.5°C Overshoot
entry.content:
Hacker News Best | unric.org | source | hacker news

The United Nations Environment Programme has published its 2026 Emissions Gap Report, warning that the Paris Agreement goal of limiting global warming to 1.5°C is no longer achievable within the decade. Titled "The Point of Return," the report states that exceeding the 1.5°C threshold is now imminent and unavoidable, requiring a new strategy to limit peak warming and bring temperatures back down by the end of the century.

To keep warming below 2°C and eventually return to 1.5°C, the report outlines that global greenhouse gas emissions must fall by 18 percent by 2030, 45 percent by 2035, and 69 percent by 2040 relative to 2025 levels. Current national climate commitments fall significantly short of these benchmarks, achieving only modest reductions and highlighting a severe leadership gap in global climate action.

Programmer and soon-to-be father Steve Krouse explores the evolving purpose of education as artificial general intelligence (AGI) reshapes traditional skill sets and career trajectories. Reflecting on how his own economic value as a software developer feels compromised, he questions what knowledge and values remain vital to impart to the next generation.

Drawing on Neil Postman’s 1995 book The End of Education and historical false alarms regarding educational technology—such as Thomas Edison’s 1913 prediction that books would become obsolete—Krouse examines how institutional schooling endures through shifting societal needs. Ultimately, he suggests that as traditional economic incentives wobble, parents and educators must collaboratively forge new narratives and purposes for learning.
